examInfo.format: The official GED site lists the Social Studies test as 70 minutes in 1 part with no break (including 2 minutes of instructions and final review) and an on-screen calculator. Question types include multiple choice, drag and drop, select an area, and drop-down. GED Testing Service's Assessment Guide says about 50% of the test is civics and government, 20% United States history, 15% economics, and 15% geography and the world, and that about half of the questions come in sets of two or three about one passage, map, or graph. The test gives you the facts you need in the passages; you are not asked to memorize dates or define terms from memory. GED Testing Service does not publish a fixed number of questions on its site; this practice mock uses 40 four-choice questions (20 civics and government, 8 U.S. history, 6 economics, 6 geography and the world) in 70 minutes. All questions on this site are original AI-written practice questions.

passCriteria.description: The real test is scored on a scale of 100 to 200, and you pass with 145 or higher. GED Testing Service does not publish a percent-correct cutoff, so this site uses 65% correct as a practice goal only. It is not an official score.

content.eligibility: The GED test is for adults who did not finish high school. Age limits, residency rules, and fees are set by each state. Check your state's rules on ged.com before you schedule.
content.intro: The GED Social Studies test is one of the four GED tests you must pass to earn a high school equivalency credential. It checks whether you can read social studies passages, historical documents, maps, graphs, and tables, and reason about what they show. Half of the test is about civics and government, and the rest covers U.S. history, economics, and geography and the world. It is not a memorization test: the passages give you the details you need, and you have an on-screen calculator.
content.trendSummary: GED Testing Service builds the test from four content areas: civics and government (about 50%), United States history (about 20%), economics (about 15%), and geography and the world (about 15%). Its two focusing themes are Development of Modern Liberties and Democracy, and Dynamic Responses in Societal Systems, so expect topics such as the principles of American democracy, the three branches and checks and balances, the Bill of Rights, elections, key founding documents, the Civil War and civil rights, supply and demand, and how people and the environment affect each other. Many questions ask you to find the main idea of a passage, tell fact from opinion, spot an author's point of view, or read a map, chart, or graph.
content.studyTip: Spend the most time on civics and government, because it is about half the test. Learn the basic ideas, such as separation of powers, checks and balances, federalism, and what the main amendments protect, but do not try to memorize every date. Practice reading short historical passages and asking what the author wants and what evidence supports the idea, and practice reading tables, line graphs, and supply and demand graphs.

faqs.question: What score do I need to pass GED Social Studies?
faqs.answer: The GED site says you need 145 out of 200 on each test, including Social Studies. GED Testing Service does not publish how many questions you must get right, so this site uses 65% correct as a practice goal.

faqs.question: How long is the GED Social Studies test?
faqs.answer: The official GED site lists 70 minutes in one part with no break. That time includes about 2 minutes for instructions and a final review.

faqs.question: Do I need to memorize dates and capitals for GED Social Studies?
faqs.answer: No. The GED site says you will not need to memorize the capitals of countries or the dates of events. You will be given information about an event and asked to use it to draw conclusions. Knowing the basic ideas of U.S. government and history still makes the passages much easier to read.

faqs.question: Is there an essay on the GED Social Studies test?
faqs.answer: No. GED Testing Service removed the Social Studies extended response (essay) question in 2016. The written essay is part of the Reasoning Through Language Arts test.

faqs.question: Are these real GED questions?
faqs.answer: No. GED Testing Service does not publish its test questions. Every question on this site is an original AI-written practice question based on the official content topics, and they may contain errors. Please report anything that looks wrong.

studyTips.studyOrder: Start with Civics and Government, because it is about half of the test. In that area, Structure of U.S. Government and Democratic Principles and Types of Government carry the most weight in this site's outline, followed by Rights and Responsibilities. Then study U.S. History (about 20%), and finish with Economics and Geography and the World (about 15% each).
studyTips.hardChapters: In Structure of U.S. Government, make a small chart of which branch checks which, because vetoes, overrides, judicial review, and Senate approval are easy to mix up. In Rights and Responsibilities, match each common amendment (First, Fourth, Fifth, Sixth, Eighth) to one example. In Microeconomics and Macroeconomics, practice reading a supply and demand graph by finding where the two lines cross before you look at the choices.
studyTips.examDay: You have 70 minutes in one part with no break, and about half the questions come in groups about one passage, map, or graph. Read the question first, then look in the passage or graph for the exact information it asks about. Watch for words like opinion, evidence, and point of view, and mark hard questions to come back to before time runs out.
